descriptors.title: Investigate problems for users
descriptors.description: investigate simple problems for known users that can be solved with digital systems
descriptors.knowledge: Students have not yet formally investigated problems. They have encountered digital systems in familiar contexts and can recognise when a digital system helps them do something. They have not yet structured a problem investigation — identifying a user, a problem, and how a digital system could address it.
elaborations: investigating internet-based translation tools and how similar digital tools could promote the use of First Nations Australians' languages or assist communications, for example responding to cultural stories of Australian First Nations Peoples
investigating familiar and easily understood problems with few complications or steps needed to solve them, for example deciding what to wear by checking the forecast on a weather app
identifying how digital systems are used to solve problems at school, for example taking attendance or borrowing a library book

exploring how a familiar problem could be solved using a robot, for example creating a model robot using cardboard boxes and explaining how it could be used to clean up the classroom floor at the end of the day

nodes.label: Identifying a user and their problem
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a known user and describe a simple, specific problem that user has
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a named user and a described problem, Node 2's investigation has no subject — students cannot establish what a problem involves if no user or problem has been identified.
criteria: Names a specific user (not 'everyone' or 'people')
Describes the problem from the user's perspective — what they can't do or find difficult, not what solution they want

width.minimum: Name a known user (themselves, a classmate, family member) and describe one specific problem they experience that a digital system might help solve
width.typical: Identify multiple known users across familiar contexts (home, school, community) and describe a specific, observable problem for each; confirm the problem is real by asking the user or observing directly
wider: Investigate how digital translation tools could address communication problems for First Nations Australians — identify a specific user and language communication need
Explore how a familiar community problem (e.g. knowing if the school library book you want is available) could be described as a problem for a known user

modes.reason: Students at this level often describe problems too broadly ('everyone wants to play games') or describe solutions before problems ('we need an app'). Encountering a range of specific, distinct user contexts — different people with different problems — helps students develop the habit of grounding problems in a real, named user before jumping to solutions.

nodes.label: Establishing what the problem involves
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate a simple problem by finding out what the user needs and what would count as solving it
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot describe what solving the problem would look like cannot attempt Node 3 — identifying how a digital system could solve the problem requires a success definition to match against.
criteria: Asks or answers at least one question about the problem from the user's perspective
Describes what success looks like — what the user would be able to do once the problem is solved

width.minimum: Ask at least one question to find out more about the problem from the user's perspective; describe what solving the problem would look like
width.typical: Ask the user questions to understand the problem; identify what information is needed and what success looks like; describe the problem in terms of what the user needs to be able to do
wider: Compare two versions of the same problem (e.g. 'I want to borrow a library book' — from a student's perspective vs a teacher's perspective) and identify how the problem description changes based on who the user is
Investigate a robot as a possible solution to a classroom clean-up problem — define what the robot would need to do by describing the problem in specific, step-by-step terms

modes.reason: Problem investigation at this level requires students to reason from the user's perspective rather than their own. Scaffolding the investigation (who is the user? what can't they do? what would help?) prevents students from jumping to solutions before the problem is understood. The reasoning structure is the investigation.

nodes.label: Identifying how a digital system could solve the problem
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how a digital system could solve a simple, known problem for a specific user
criteria: Names a specific digital system
Explains how the system addresses the user's stated problem — the connection between system and problem is explicit

width.minimum: Identify one digital system that could solve the user's problem and explain how it addresses the need
width.typical: Investigate how an existing or imagined digital system could solve the problem; explain which features of the system address the user's specific need; consider whether the solution actually solves the problem for that user
wider: Investigate multiple possible digital systems for the same problem — for example whether a weather app, a robot, or an alarm could each solve the same 'what to wear' problem in different ways
Explore how digital tools are used at school to solve known problems (attendance, library loans) — identify the user, the problem and how the system addresses it

modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate user identification, problem description, and digital system knowledge simultaneously. The investigation is complete when all three elements are connected — the system is matched to the user's specific problem. Integration failure looks like: naming a system that doesn't address the stated problem, or identifying a solution before establishing the problem.

descriptors.title: Follow and describe algorithms
descriptors.description: follow and describe algorithms involving a sequence of steps, branching (decisions) and iteration (repetition)
descriptors.knowledge: This is the first algorithmic thinking descriptor in the DT curriculum (no Foundation predecessor). Students bring general sequencing experience from everyday tasks — they can order familiar actions. They have not yet used computational vocabulary (sequence, branching, iteration) or applied algorithmic structure to a problem.
elaborations: following a short, ordered sequence of steps and making decisions to solve a simple problem, for example follow a recipe or directions to reach a location
describing the steps and decisions (in the correct order) needed to solve a simple problem, for example writing, saying, drawing or photographing the steps needed to make a sandwich
rearranging into the correct order a series of mixed-up pictures that describe a story, for example stories authored and published by First Nations Australians
identifying the steps needed to solve a problem, and understanding when their order is important, for example socks must be put on before shoes but a jumper can be put on before or after shoes
identifying the decisions needed to solve a problem and the next steps to follow in each case, for example if it is raining, take a raincoat, otherwise take a hat
following algorithms that repeat a single step a fixed number of times, for example practise spelling a word 5 times or throw and catch a ball with a partner 10 times

nodes.label: Following and describing sequences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow a short ordered sequence of steps and describe the steps in correct order
nodes.hinge_reason: Sequence fluency is the foundation for all subsequent structural types — the reason explicitly states that rushing to decisions before sequence is automatic leads to confused algorithms. Students who cannot hold step order reliably cannot add branching or iteration without losing the sequence structure.
criteria: Follows a sequence of steps in the correct order without skipping or repeating
Describes steps in order using sequencing language (first, then, next, last)

width.minimum: Follow a provided 4–6 step sequence to complete a simple task; describe the steps in order using first/then/next/last
width.typical: Follow and describe sequences for multiple familiar tasks (making a sandwich, getting ready for school, feeding a pet); rearrange mixed-up steps into the correct order; explain why order matters
wider: Rearrange a mixed-up sequence of pictures from a story authored and published by First Nations Australians — describe the correct order and explain how each step leads to the next
Compare two tasks where step order matters (socks before shoes) and two where it does not (jumper before or after shoes) — explain the difference

modes.reason: Correct sequencing requires precision — students at this age need repeated practice ordering steps across varied contexts before branching and iteration are introduced. Rushing to decisions before sequence is automatic leads to confused algorithms that mix step types.

nodes.label: Identifying and following branching (decisions)
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify decision points in an algorithm and follow the correct path based on the condition
nodes.hinge_reason: Branching is the hardest structural element and the reason explicitly describes systematic errors (describing only one path). Students who cannot hold both paths simultaneously cannot attempt Node 4's integration of all three structures.
criteria: Identifies a decision point and states the condition being checked
Follows the correct path for a given condition and can explain both possible outcomes

width.minimum: Given an algorithm with one decision point (if/otherwise), follow the correct path based on the condition; explain what decision is being made and what each outcome means
width.typical: Follow and describe algorithms with multiple decision points across familiar contexts (weather → what to wear, if raining → raincoat, otherwise → hat); draw or explain the decision structure; identify the condition and both possible outcomes
wider: Create an algorithm for a classroom decision (e.g. if the book is in the library, borrow it, otherwise put it on the wish list) — identify the condition, the two paths, and the outcome of each
Apply decision-making to a recipe or process — identify where choices are made and what each choice leads to

modes.reason: Branching is the hardest structural element to grasp at this level — students often describe only one path of a decision (the if, not the otherwise) or confuse the condition with the action. Encountering decisions in multiple, distinct contexts (weather, library, recipe) where both paths are equally plausible helps students see that both outcomes must always be specified.

Following branching requires students to hold two possible paths in mind simultaneously and apply the condition to select one. Explicitly scaffolding the if/otherwise structure — reading it aloud, drawing both paths — prevents students from treating every decision as always taking the same path.

nodes.label: Identifying and following iteration (repetition)
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify when steps are repeated in an algorithm and follow algorithms that include a fixed-count repetition
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify the boundary of what is repeated (loop body vs surrounding sequence) cannot integrate iteration with sequence and branching in Node 4 — the structural distinction is the prerequisite for coordination.
criteria: Identifies a step or sequence that repeats in an algorithm
States how many times the repetition occurs

width.minimum: Follow an algorithm that repeats a step a fixed number of times (e.g. practise spelling a word 5 times); identify which step repeats and how many times
width.typical: Follow and describe algorithms that include fixed-count repetition across multiple familiar contexts (throw and catch 10 times, write letters 5 times); explain why repetition is used; distinguish repetition from a one-time step
wider: Create an algorithm that uses repetition for a physical activity or game (e.g. jump 3 times, then clap, then repeat) — write or draw the algorithm showing which part repeats
Compare an algorithm with repetition to one without — explain how repetition makes the algorithm shorter and more efficient

modes.reason: Students readily understand that 'do it again' means repetition, but may not identify the boundary of what is repeated — the body of the loop — vs what happens after it ends. Multiple contexts where the repeated element is clearly bounded help students distinguish the repeated part from the surrounding sequence.

nodes.label: Describing algorithms with all three structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow and describe an algorithm that combines sequence, branching and iteration
criteria: Follows an algorithm with at least two structural types without error
Describes or explains the role of at least two structural elements in the algorithm

width.minimum: Follow an algorithm that includes at least two of the three structures (sequence + branching, or sequence + iteration); describe what each structural element does
width.typical: Follow and describe algorithms that include sequence, a decision point, and repetition; explain the role of each structural type; create a simple example combining at least two types
wider: Describe a morning routine algorithm that includes sequence (steps in order), a decision (if it is cold, put on a jacket), and iteration (brush teeth for two minutes) — explain what type of structure each part is
Write, say, draw or photograph the full algorithm for a process that genuinely needs all three types — explaining each component to a partner or the class

modes.reason: At this node students must coordinate sequence, branching and iteration in a single coherent algorithm description. Integration failure looks like: correctly identifying each structure in isolation but losing track of how they combine — describing the steps but omitting the decision, or treating repetition as just 'doing it again' without connecting it to the algorithm's overall structure.

descriptors.title: Discuss existing digital systems
descriptors.description: discuss how existing digital systems satisfy identified needs for known users
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored digital systems in familiar contexts (AC9TDI2K01). They can identify systems and name their components. They have not yet evaluated systems against user needs — linking what a system does to whether it satisfies a specific user's requirement.
elaborations: describing how familiar digital systems meet the needs of individuals, for example how different family members use a tablet for different needs – to play videos, read the news or follow a recipe

discussing how we use digital systems to store and access information, and how that information helps us learn about our environment, interactions and leisure activities, for example how interactive versions of stories authored and published by First Nations Australians preserve important cultural expressions

sharing ideas about how digital systems are used at school for learning, for example sharing a student's work with the class on an interactive display screen to provide class feedback on their writing

sharing and describing ways that common digital systems can be used to meet communication needs, for example tablets can be used as phones and tools for communication between families living in different locations

nodes.label: Identifying needs for known users
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe a specific need that a known user has, distinct from a general want or preference
nodes.hinge_reason: Without an identified need for a known user, Node 2 has nothing to connect system features to — discussing how a system satisfies a need requires a need to have been established first.
criteria: Names a specific user
Describes a need linked to a task or purpose, not just a preference

width.minimum: For one known user (themselves, a family member, a classmate), describe a specific need that a digital system could help with
width.typical: Identify needs for multiple different users across home, school and community contexts; distinguish a need (something required to do a task) from a want (a preference)
wider: Discuss how digital systems store and provide access to cultural stories authored and published by First Nations Australians — identify the need these systems satisfy for communities who want to preserve and share these stories

Compare what a student needs from a digital system (e.g. to watch videos, play games) with what a teacher needs from the same system (e.g. to share work with the class) — identify the different needs for the same device

modes.reason: Students at this level tend to describe all digital system use as want-based ('I want to play games') rather than identifying genuine needs. Multiple users across contrasting contexts — student vs teacher, home vs community — help students see that the same system can address different, specific needs depending on the user.

nodes.label: Discussing how systems satisfy needs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how an existing digital system satisfies an identified need — connecting system features to the user's need
criteria: Names a feature of the digital system (not just the system type)
Explains how that feature addresses the user's identified need

width.minimum: For one known user and one identified need, discuss at least one feature of a digital system and explain how it addresses the need
width.typical: Discuss how multiple features of a digital system satisfy different aspects of a user's need; share and compare ideas with the class about how systems are used for learning, communication and access to information
wider: Discuss how an interactive display screen in the classroom satisfies the need for sharing student work — identify what specific features (large screen, visibility, connection to other devices) address different aspects of the need
Discuss how tablets can be used as phones and communication tools between families in different locations — identify the needs satisfied and which features of the tablet make this possible

modes.reason: Discussing how a system satisfies a need requires students to reason about the fit between a specific feature and a specific need. Without scaffolding (what is the need? what does the system do? how does that match?), students tend to simply describe the system without connecting it to the user's need — the fit relationship is the challenging cognitive step.

descriptors.title: Create and communicate content
descriptors.description: use the basic features of common digital tools to create, locate and communicate content
descriptors.knowledge: This is the first content creation descriptor (no Foundation predecessor). Students have used digital systems in familiar contexts and can recognise what they are used for. They have not yet deliberately used digital tools to create original content, locate specific content, or communicate content to others.
elaborations: using familiar digital systems to create content with others, for example using presentation software to retell a story
taking, storing safely and presenting photos of class work, for example locating photos they took of their work to show to parents or carers or for the teacher to upload to the class shared folder
finding images of (local) Australian flora and fauna or places for use in a story and including First Nations Australians' names for the items
using a camera or drawing app to create a picture, for example making a card for a family member that includes a photo and short message
creating individual pieces of work that contribute to a group task, for example each student contributes a recipe and photo of their favourite food to create a class recipe book

nodes.label: Using basic features to create content
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the basic features of a common digital tool to create a piece of content
nodes.hinge_reason: Procedural fluency with creation features is prerequisite for Node 2 — students who stall on feature access during creation cannot redirect attention to locating and retrieving content.
criteria: Uses at least one basic feature of a digital tool to produce original content
The content produced is accessible — saved or stored so it can be found again

width.minimum: Use at least one basic feature of a digital tool (camera, drawing app, text input, presentation software) to create a piece of original content
width.typical: Use basic features across different content types (take a photo, draw a picture, type a message, add text to a presentation) using appropriate tools; save or store the created content
wider: Use presentation software to retell a story — apply features to combine text and pictures to communicate the story sequence
Create a card for a family member using a camera or drawing app — include a photo and a short typed message, combining two creation features

modes.reason: Feature use at this level requires motor accuracy and procedural memory — selecting the right icon, saving correctly, locating saved work. Students need repeated practice with the same features across multiple creation tasks before fluency develops. Consolidation here prevents stalling on procedural steps when communicating content.

nodes.label: Using basic features to locate content
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the basic features of a digital tool to locate specific content — including stored files and online images
nodes.hinge_reason: Content that cannot be located cannot be communicated — Node 3 requires students to find and organise content before sharing it. Navigational failure at Node 2 collapses the Node 3 communication task.
criteria: Locates at least one piece of content (stored file or online image) relevant to the task
Can show or explain where the content was found

width.minimum: Use a basic feature of a digital tool to locate one piece of stored or online content relevant to a task (e.g. find a saved photo, find an image of a plant or animal)
width.typical: Locate stored files (photos of their own work) and find images online for a purpose (local flora and fauna, places); explain how they found the content and what they used it for
wider: Find images of Australian flora and fauna including First Nations Australians' names for the items — use the images in a story or presentation, crediting the source
Take photos of class work and locate them in a class shared folder — demonstrate that stored content can be found and used again later

modes.reason: Locating content involves navigating file systems, folders and browser interfaces — procedural skills that require accurate execution. Students commonly lose their saved content or cannot find it again. Repeated practice locating and retrieving content builds the navigational fluency needed for subsequent communication tasks.

nodes.label: Using basic features to communicate content
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the basic features of a digital tool to communicate created or located content to others
criteria: Communicates content to at least one other person using a digital tool
The content shared is the intended content — not accidentally shared, not the wrong file

width.minimum: Use a digital tool to share or present a piece of content to at least one other person (show a photo, present a slide, share a message)
width.typical: Create individual content contributions that form part of a group task — for example contributing a recipe and photo to a class recipe book; present or share completed content with the class or a family member
wider: Contribute a recipe and photo of a favourite food to a class digital recipe book — explain how individual contributions combine to create a shared piece of content
Use presentation software to show class work on an interactive display — explain what the content shows and respond to feedback

modes.reason: Communication requires students to coordinate creation (produce content), location (find or organise it) and presentation (share it with others). At this node, the three activities — create, locate, communicate — must work together. Integration failure looks like: content exists but cannot be found to share, or content is shared but is incomplete or unintended.

descriptors.title: Share content and collaborate
descriptors.description: use the basic features of common digital tools to share content and collaborate demonstrating agreed behaviours, guided by trusted adults
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use basic features of digital tools to create, locate and communicate content (AC9TDI2P04). They have not yet applied agreed behaviours when sharing digitally, nor considered personal safety and privacy when sharing online with others.
elaborations: taking and sharing photos of class work with parents or carers using classroom messaging software with teacher guidance

applying agreed standards of behaviour when sharing content with classmates, for example using language that is considered by all students and the teacher to be appropriate when they are writing messages to each other
considering the need for online safety when sharing information, for example recognising that personal information such as a photo can be used inappropriately

nodes.label: Applying agreed behaviours when sharing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and apply agreed behaviours when sharing content with classmates using digital tools
criteria: Identifies at least one agreed behaviour for digital sharing
Applies the agreed behaviour when sharing content — content and language are appropriate

width.minimum: Identify at least one agreed behaviour for sharing content digitally (e.g. appropriate language, asking permission before sharing someone's photo); apply the behaviour when sharing content with a classmate
width.typical: Apply agreed standards of behaviour across a sharing context — appropriate language in messages, respectful presentation of class work, checking what is and isn't appropriate to share; explain why the agreed behaviours matter
wider: Take and share photos of class work with parents or carers using classroom messaging software — apply agreed behaviours with teacher guidance and explain what was appropriate to share and why
Discuss as a class what standards of behaviour everyone agrees on for digital messages — identify examples of appropriate and inappropriate content and explain the reasoning

modes.reason: Students understand 'be kind' in person but often do not transfer this to digital contexts. Encountering agreed behaviours across multiple sharing situations (messaging classmates, sharing photos with parents, presenting work) builds the generalised understanding that digital sharing requires the same social standards as in-person interaction.

nodes.label: Recognising personal information and online safety
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify examples of personal information and recognise that sharing personal information online requires care
criteria: Names at least one type of personal information correctly
Explains at least one reason why that information should be shared carefully

width.minimum: Identify at least one type of personal information (photo, name, address) and state why it should be shared carefully online
width.typical: Give examples of personal information that could be used inappropriately if shared; explain that some information (photos, addresses, phone numbers) needs permission before being shared; identify who trusted adults are and their role in guiding online sharing
wider: Discuss scenarios where personal information was shared without permission — explain what could go wrong and what to do if it happens
Compare what information it is safe to share with classmates on a classroom platform versus what should only be shared with family — identify who the trusted adult is in each context

modes.reason: Recognising personal information risk requires students to reason about consequence — not just 'what is personal information' but 'why does sharing it matter and to whom'. Scaffolding the reasoning (who could see it? what could they do with it? who should I ask?) prevents students from treating all sharing as equally safe or equally dangerous.

descriptors.title: Access accounts with credentials
descriptors.description: access their school account with a recorded username and password
descriptors.knowledge: Students have used digital systems at home and school but have not previously managed personal login credentials. They may have used shared devices without individual accounts. They have not yet connected the concept of personal credentials to privacy or account ownership.
elaborations: using username and password recorded in a private place to access a digital system, for example logging into a school computer using details given on a card by the teacher

nodes.label: What accounts and credentials are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what a username and password are and why they are used to access a digital system
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand why credentials exist (privacy and identity) will execute Node 2 login as a rote procedure without any safety awareness — they cannot reason about credential privacy if the purpose of credentials is opaque.
criteria: Can explain what a username is and what a password is
Can state at least one reason why credentials are kept private

width.minimum: Explain what a username and password are; state why they are used to access a system (to identify the user and keep their account private)
width.typical: Explain that a username identifies you and a password keeps your account private; give examples of where accounts are used at school (computer login, school website); explain that credentials are personal — not shared with others
wider: Compare using a library card (physical identification) with a username and password (digital identification) — explain what each one does and why both serve the same purpose of identifying the user
Discuss what would happen if someone else used your username and password — explain why keeping credentials private protects your account

modes.reason: Students may not have a conceptual model for why credentials exist — they experience login as a procedural requirement, not as a privacy and identity mechanism. Multiple contexts that ground the purpose of credentials (library card analogy, school login, account protection scenarios) help students understand why the procedure exists, not just how to follow it.

nodes.label: Accessing a school account with recorded credentials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a recorded username and password to access their school account
criteria: Successfully logs into the school system using their recorded credentials
Enters the username and password in the correct fields

width.minimum: Use a recorded username and password (e.g. from a card given by the teacher) to log into a school digital system
width.typical: Access a school account using recorded credentials; locate the login screen; enter the username and password accurately; access their personal account area
wider: Limited width — this is a narrow procedural skill. The genuine extension is understanding why credentials are private and personal (covered in node 1 and in AC9TDI2P07).

modes.reason: Accurate credential entry is a procedural skill requiring motor precision — distinguishing username from password fields, entering characters correctly, locating the login screen. Students need practice to build fluency. Consolidation is the appropriate response when errors are procedural (wrong field, typos, forgotten steps) rather than conceptual.

descriptors.title: Personal data stored online
descriptors.description: discuss that some websites and apps store their personal data online
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that credentials are personal and private (AC9TDI2P06). They can identify some types of personal information (AC9TDI2P05). They have not yet discussed the concept that websites and apps collect and store personal data online — or that entering details online creates a stored record.
elaborations: sharing examples of the data collected by apps and websites they commonly use, for example usernames and email addresses used by school websites and games to log in
discussing the importance of asking permission from a parent or carer before entering personal details online such as address, phone number and date of birth

nodes.label: What data websites and apps collect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can give examples of the types of personal data that websites and apps commonly collect
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name the types of data that apps collect cannot reason in Node 2 about why permission is needed before entering specific details — the permission reasoning requires knowing what is at stake.
criteria: Names at least two types of data that apps or websites collect
Gives at least one specific example from an app or website they know

width.minimum: Name at least two types of data that websites or apps collect (e.g. username, email address, date of birth) from examples they commonly encounter
width.typical: Give examples of data collected by apps and websites they commonly use — usernames and email addresses for school websites and games; explain that entering this information creates a record that is stored by the website or app
wider: Compare what data two different platforms collect — for example a school website versus an online game — and explain what each collects and why
Discuss what information is needed just to use an app versus what might be optional — identify what is necessary and what might be sharing more than needed

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of examples of data that apps collect — a single example (username) is insufficient to build a reliable understanding of the range of personal data at stake. Repeated examples across different platforms build the recognition that many different types of information are collected across different contexts.

nodes.label: The importance of asking permission before entering personal details
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss why it is important to ask a parent or carer before entering personal details online
criteria: States at least one reason why asking permission before entering personal details is important
Identifies a trusted adult as the person to ask

width.minimum: State at least one reason why asking a parent or carer before entering personal details online is important
width.typical: Discuss why personal details like address, phone number and date of birth require permission before being shared online; explain that once stored, data may be used in ways that are not immediately obvious; identify the trusted adult role in guiding these decisions
wider: Discuss a scenario: an online game asks for your home address to send you a prize — explain what to do and why, referencing the trusted adult principle

Compare asking permission to enter details online with other safety rules at school (e.g. not leaving the school grounds) — identify that both involve a trusted adult because consequences may not be immediately visible to the child

modes.reason: Reasoning about why permission matters requires students to think about downstream consequence — data stored now can be used later in ways that are not immediately obvious. Scaffolding the reasoning (who stores it? what could they do with it? why does a trusted adult know more about this?) prevents students from treating 'ask a trusted adult' as an arbitrary rule rather than a protective one.

descriptors.title: Define problems with user stories
descriptors.description: define problems with given design criteria and by co-creating user stories
descriptors.knowledge: Students can investigate simple problems for known users that can be solved with digital systems (AC9TDI2P01). They have explored what makes a problem solvable. They have not yet worked with explicit design criteria or user story formats as structured tools for problem definition.
elaborations: recognising a range of familiar problems and defining achievable solutions using given design criteria, for example buying presents for family members within a specified budget
using responses to guiding questions to write a user story, for example a family member wants a way of entertaining their puppy when they are at school to stop it digging holes
co-creating a user story using a template such as 'A has so that ', for example 'a sports team wants to access league rankings online so that they can see their progress'

developing a problem statement for collecting and managing information, for example how First Nations Australians rangers could monitor animal populations, such as local marine turtles, using global positioning systems (GPS)
co-creating user stories about exploring hard-to-reach locations, for example a school student wants to explore neighbouring countries classified as remote to compare how people live

nodes.label: What design criteria are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read a set of given design criteria and explain what a solution must do to meet them
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot interpret design criteria cannot check in N3 whether their user story and criteria are consistent — the integration task requires reading criteria correctly.
criteria: Reads given criteria and restates what a solution must do
Does not confuse criteria (what it must do) with a solution (what it will be)

width.minimum: Given a set of design criteria for a simple problem, list what a solution would need to do to satisfy them
width.typical: Read given design criteria across different problem contexts (a game, a tool, a communication solution); explain in plain language what each criterion means for what the solution must do
wider: Explore design criteria for digital tools used by First Nations rangers — discuss how criteria like reliability in remote areas or low data usage reflect the specific context of users
Compare two sets of design criteria for the same problem — discuss how different criteria lead to different solutions and why criteria choices matter

nodes.label: User story structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a user story using a template that identifies who the user is, what they need, and why
nodes.hinge_reason: A malformed user story (missing user, need or purpose) leaves nothing to check criteria against in N3 — the integration collapses if the user story is a stub.
criteria: Completes all three parts of a user story template
User is a specific person or group, not a generic description ('everyone')

width.minimum: Complete a user story template ('A [user] wants [need] so that [reason]') for a familiar, simple problem
width.typical: Co-create user stories for a range of simple problem contexts; identify the user, need and purpose for each; refine a user story when the 'so that' reason is missing or unclear
wider: Write user stories from the perspective of users in different circumstances — for example, a First Nations student in a remote community who wants to explore neighbouring countries to compare how people live; discuss how context shapes the user story
Investigate user stories for problems involving non-human users (e.g. a ranger group monitoring turtle populations) — discuss whether user stories still work and what changes

modes.reason: Students who write user stories for only familiar contexts (their own problems) often struggle to write from an unfamiliar user's perspective. Practice across diverse user contexts builds the habit of identifying with users rather than projecting own needs.

nodes.label: Defining a problem using both tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use design criteria and a user story together to define a problem — stating what the solution must do and who it is for
criteria: Writes a user story with a named user, need and purpose
States at least two design criteria consistent with the user story

width.minimum: Given a problem context, co-create a user story and identify two design criteria the solution must meet
width.typical: Define problems across different contexts using user stories and design criteria together; check that the criteria are consistent with the needs identified in the user story
wider: Define a problem involving data collection for a community need (e.g. monitoring local wildlife populations) — write user stories from multiple user perspectives and derive design criteria that satisfy all of them
Explore a problem from a First Nations context (e.g. using digital tools to document cultural knowledge) — discuss how the user story and criteria might differ from a mainstream educational tool

modes.reason: This node asks students to hold design criteria and user stories in relation — checking that criteria actually capture what the user needs. The integration step (do the criteria follow from the user story?) is a reasoning move that needs explicit practice.

descriptors.title: Algorithms with branching and iteration
descriptors.description: follow and describe algorithms involving sequencing, comparison operators (branching) and iteration
descriptors.knowledge: Students can follow and describe algorithms involving a sequence of steps, branching and iteration (AC9TDI2P02). They have encountered these three structures but at a descriptive, recognition level. They have not yet worked with comparison operators explicitly or described algorithms involving numerical conditions.
elaborations: following the steps and decisions of algorithms and knowing what step they are up to, for example following rules to form the past tense of regular verbs such as 'create' to 'created', 'try' to 'tried' and 'cook' to 'cooked' and checking off items on a list as they are completed
describing algorithms using representations such as a list of steps or a diagram, for example drawing a diagram of a recipe involving decisions

understanding there can be more than one sequence of steps to solve a problem, some are better than others, and the steps should be unambiguous, for example describing 2 different ways to get to the same location
describing the decisions needed to solve a problem, including numerical and text comparisons, for example if the UV index is above 3, put on sunscreen and a hat
describing algorithms that repeat steps a fixed number of times, for example calculating multiplication using repeated addition, where the sum changes in each iteration

nodes.label: Sequencing as ordered steps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow a multi-step algorithm and identify where they are in the sequence
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot track their position in a sequence cannot attempt N2 or N3 — branching and iteration both require knowing where you are in the algorithm before deciding or repeating.
criteria: Follows a multi-step algorithm without skipping steps
Can identify which step they are at when asked mid-sequence

width.minimum: Follow a written or diagrammatic algorithm with at least four steps; identify the current step when paused mid-sequence
width.typical: Follow algorithms in different representations (list of steps, simple diagram, recipe format); track progress through the sequence; identify if a step has been skipped and what effect that has
wider: Follow algorithms that describe First Nations Australian practices with strict ordering requirements (e.g. step sequences for preparing traditional foods or caring for specific animals) — discuss why step order matters in these contexts
Compare two algorithms for the same task with different step orders — identify which is more efficient or which produces better results and explain why

nodes.label: Comparison operators as branching conditions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe a branch in an algorithm using a comparison operator (e.g. if UV index > 3, if score = 10) and explain what each path does
nodes.hinge_reason: Comparison operators are directly prerequisite for implementing branching in AC9TDI4P04 — students who cannot identify the condition and trace both paths cannot write a working conditional program.
criteria: Correctly traces both branches of an algorithm with a comparison condition
Names the comparison operator (greater than, equal to, etc.) used in the branch

width.minimum: Given an algorithm with one branch using a comparison (e.g. if temperature is above 25°C), trace both paths and describe what happens in each case
width.typical: Describe algorithms with multiple branches using comparison operators (greater than, less than, equal to) involving numbers and text; trace the correct path for different input values
wider: Describe algorithms that branch on comparisons involving culturally specific conditions — for example, IF a certain animal is found in a ranger survey THEN a specific protocol applies; discuss how the comparison drives the decision
Explore algorithms involving combined conditions (e.g. IF UV index > 3 AND it is a school day) — describe what the combined comparison checks for

modes.reason: Comparison operators abstract quickly from the concrete case. Students who only see one type of comparison (e.g. 'greater than' with temperature) may not recognise that text comparisons, equal-to checks, and multi-condition branches follow the same logic. Multiple contexts build the generalised pattern.

Tracing both branches of a conditional requires holding two cases simultaneously. Students benefit from explicit scaffolding: 'what happens if the condition is true? what happens if it is false?' before attempting to write their own branches.

nodes.label: Iteration as repeating steps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe an algorithm that repeats steps a fixed number of times and explain what changes with each repetition
criteria: Identifies that steps are repeated in an iterative algorithm
States what changes between repetitions (e.g. a count increases, a position moves)

width.minimum: Follow an algorithm that repeats a step a set number of times (e.g. add a number 5 times to compute a product); describe what the algorithm does and what changes in each repetition
width.typical: Describe algorithms with iteration for different purposes — fixed-count repetition (multiply using repeated addition), and repetition until a condition is met; identify what is constant and what changes across iterations
wider: Describe iteration in algorithms used for monitoring tasks — for example, an algorithm that counts sightings of a specific animal in a survey by repeating a tally step; discuss how the repetition connects to the data being collected
Explore an algorithm that combines iteration and branching — describe how repetition and decisions interact (e.g. 'check each item on a list; IF it matches THEN record it')

modes.reason: Students often understand iteration from one context (e.g. counting) but do not recognise it in others (processing a list, animating movement, repeating a procedure). Multiple contexts build a functional understanding of 'do this repeatedly' across varied algorithmic uses.

nodes.label: Describing complete algorithms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe an algorithm that combines sequencing, branching and iteration in their own words or using a diagram
criteria: Identifies at least one example each of sequencing, branching and iteration in a described algorithm
Description matches what the algorithm actually does

width.minimum: Given an algorithm with all three structures, describe what it does in plain language — identifying where the sequence is, where a decision occurs, and where repetition happens
width.typical: Describe algorithms of different complexity using written descriptions and diagrams; explain the purpose of the algorithm and how each structure contributes to achieving it
wider: Describe an algorithm for a First Nations ranger protocol that involves all three structures — for example, a monitoring procedure with a fixed number of survey loops, conditional recording rules, and sequential reporting steps
Describe and compare two algorithms that solve the same problem differently (e.g. two routes to the same location with different decision points) — explain why both are valid and how they differ

modes.reason: Describing a combined algorithm requires recognising that sequencing, branching and iteration are not separate things but work together in a single logical structure. The integration challenge is seeing how the structures interlock — this node is where that coordination is the learning.

descriptors.title: Generate, communicate and compare designs
descriptors.description: generate, communicate and compare designs
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored problems for known users and generated simple design ideas through describing, drawing or modelling (AC9TDE2P01 — Design Technologies equivalent; AC9TDI2P01 for DT problem investigation). They have not yet worked with explicit comparison of design ideas against user stories or design criteria.
elaborations: brainstorming possible design ideas and discussing these with their peers, for example sketching different ideas for a computer game
discussing whether the needs identified from the user story are met by generated design ideas, for example comparing design ideas in pairs for encouraging people to recycle

ideating multiple design ideas and comparing them against user stories, for example as a class, discussing the needs identified from the user story and brainstorming multiple design ideas (accepting all suggestions as possibilities)

nodes.label: Generating multiple design ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate more than one design idea for a given problem and describe what each idea proposes
nodes.hinge_reason: Students with only one design idea cannot meaningfully compare in N3 — comparison requires at least two distinct ideas. Convergence on a single idea makes the evaluation step trivial.
criteria: Produces at least two visibly different design ideas
Describes what each idea would do, not just what it would look like

width.minimum: Generate at least two different design ideas for a simple problem and sketch or describe each one
width.typical: Brainstorm multiple design ideas for a problem, accepting all suggestions as possibilities; describe each idea in enough detail to distinguish it from the others
wider: Generate design ideas for a problem with a First Nations Australian community context — explore how different ideas might reflect different cultural considerations or access constraints

Use a structured brainstorming technique (e.g. SCAMPER or random prompt) to generate ideas beyond obvious solutions — discuss how forced variation produces ideas that wouldn't emerge from direct thinking

modes.reason: Students in early design experience tend to converge on the first idea they think of. Generating ideas for varied problem contexts builds the habit of ideating before selecting — a phase-critical behaviour for the design cycle.

nodes.label: Communicating design ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can communicate a design idea to peers clearly enough for others to understand what it proposes
criteria: Another student can describe back what the design proposes
Includes at least one feature that addresses the user's need

width.minimum: Sketch or describe one design idea so that a peer can understand what the solution would do
width.typical: Communicate design ideas using sketches, annotations or verbal explanation; include enough detail about what the solution does, who it is for, and how users interact with it
wider: Communicate a design idea that would work for users in an unfamiliar context (e.g. a tool for a ranger group) — discuss what extra information a person unfamiliar with the context would need to understand the design
Compare different modes of communicating a design (sketch vs verbal description vs labelled diagram) — discuss which modes are clearest for different audiences

nodes.label: Comparing designs against user stories and criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare at least two design ideas against user stories and design criteria and give reasons for preferring one
criteria: Names at least one criterion or user story element when comparing designs
States a preference and connects it to a reason beyond personal taste

width.minimum: Given two design ideas and a user story, state which idea better meets the user's need and give one reason linked to the user story or a criterion
width.typical: Compare multiple design ideas against user stories and criteria for a range of problem contexts; identify which ideas meet the criteria and which miss aspects of the user's need; provide reasons for judgements
wider: Compare designs for a problem where different users have different needs — for example, a recycling encouragement tool used by different age groups — discuss how a design that suits one user story might not suit another
Explore what happens when no design idea fully meets all criteria — discuss how to decide between imperfect options and whether criteria can be prioritised

modes.reason: Comparing against criteria requires students to make a judgement move — not just describe the designs but evaluate them against a standard. The reasoning scaffold (does this design meet criterion X? does that one?) prevents students from selecting on preference alone.

This node integrates the design ideas generated in node 1 with the user stories and criteria from AC9TDI4P01. The comparison task only works when students bring both design ideas and problem definition together — coordination across the design process is the learning.

descriptors.title: Implement visual programs
descriptors.description: implement simple algorithms as visual programs involving control structures and input
descriptors.knowledge: Students can follow and describe algorithms involving sequencing, branching and iteration (AC9TDI4P02). They have described these structures but have not yet implemented them in a programming environment. They have not yet written programs that accept user input.
elaborations: writing and editing programs to solve simple problems using branching and simple iteration in a visual programming environment, for example helping a user understand multiplication by displaying the repeated addition in order
writing programs that take input from the user or environment, for example asking the user for their name and displaying it or sensing the temperature from the environment to make a decision
writing programs that make decisions involving comparison, for example comparing whether the temperature is above 25 degrees Celsius to label the weather hot or cold
writing programs that repeat one or more steps a fixed number of times, for example writing a program that displays repetitive song lyrics, such as in 'Ten in the bed'
running and testing a program to check it performs as expected, for example a character: 1. moves forward 2. turns left 3. moves forward

implementing a program that demonstrates the strict routines and techniques followed by First Nations Australian ranger groups when caring for or handling specific native animals, for example using IF and THEN statements to create a training manual, such as: IF  is injured THEN the ranger will

nodes.label: Writing and running a sequential program
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a program that executes steps in order and run it to check it performs as expected
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably sequence blocks and run programs cannot add branching or iteration — both require a functioning sequential program as the base. Fluency here is directly prerequisite for N2 and N3.
criteria: Program runs without errors
Steps execute in the correct order

width.minimum: Write a program with at least three sequential steps, run it, and confirm it performs each step in the correct order
width.typical: Write and run sequential programs across simple tasks (moving a character, displaying messages, performing calculations); identify what step the program is on when paused
wider: Implement a sequential program that enacts a specific ordered procedure — for example, the strict steps a First Nations ranger follows when handling a specific native animal; discuss why the order must be preserved in the program
Write the same sequential program in two different visual environments (e.g. Scratch and a flowchart tool) and compare how each represents the same logic

modes.reason: Writing and running sequential programs is the foundational capability for all subsequent programming work in this descriptor. Students need procedural fluency — the ability to reliably sequence blocks and interpret run output — before branching and input are introduced. Practice and precision here matter more than breadth.

nodes.label: Adding branching to programs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a program that uses a comparison condition to branch and execute different steps depending on the result
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only test one branch path (or don't recognise when a branch fires) produce programs that appear to work but fail on untested inputs — this pattern of partial testing cascades into N4 where combined structures amplify the problem.
criteria: Program executes different code depending on the condition value
Both branches produce a correct and distinct output when tested

width.minimum: Write a program with one IF/THEN branch using a comparison (e.g. if temperature > 25) that produces different outputs for different input values
width.typical: Write programs with comparison-based branches for different contexts — labelling weather as hot or cold, deciding whether to wear sunscreen, responding to a user's answer in a quiz; test the program with values that trigger each path
wider: Implement a program with IF/THEN statements based on a real protocol — for example, IF a specific animal is found injured THEN the ranger follows a specific procedure; discuss how programs can encode decision-making knowledge
Write a program with multiple conditions (IF...ELSE IF...ELSE) for a context with more than two outcomes and explain how each condition is evaluated

modes.reason: Students often test their branching program with only one input value and assume it works. Wider task contexts that require testing both branches — and later multiple branches — build the habit of checking conditional logic exhaustively.

nodes.label: Adding iteration to programs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a program that repeats steps a fixed number of times and explain what changes with each repetition
criteria: Loop executes the correct number of times
Program produces the expected output after the loop completes

width.minimum: Write a program that repeats a step a set number of times (e.g. displaying repeated song lyrics, computing a sum using repeated addition); confirm it repeats the correct number of times
width.typical: Write programs using fixed-count loops for different purposes (repeated display, repeated addition, repeated movement); identify what changes across repetitions and what stays constant
wider: Write a program that uses a loop to process multiple inputs (e.g. asking for a user's name and responding to each) — discuss how loops reduce the need to repeat code manually
Implement a program that uses both a loop and a branch — for example, a loop that counts and branches when a condition is reached; discuss how the structures combine

modes.reason: Students who only see loops in one context (e.g. printing repeated text) may not recognise that the same structure applies to movement, calculation and input processing. Multiple task contexts build generalised understanding of iteration as a structure.

nodes.label: Writing programs with user input
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a program that takes input from the user or environment and uses it in the program's logic
criteria: Program reads at least one user or environmental input
The input affects what the program does or displays

width.minimum: Write a program that accepts one piece of user input (e.g. a name or a number) and uses it in the output or a decision
width.typical: Write programs that take user input or sense environmental input (temperature, location) and use it in decisions or displays; test with different inputs to confirm the program responds correctly
wider: Write a program that takes input from both a user and the environment — for example, combining a user-entered location with a temperature sensor reading to produce a context-specific response
Implement a program where user input modifies iteration — for example, the user enters how many times a step should repeat; discuss how this makes the program more general-purpose

modes.reason: User input integrates all three control structures — input values feed into conditions (branching) and can control loops (iteration), all within a sequential program structure. This node is where students coordinate input with previously learned structures, and the coordination is the key learning.

descriptors.title: Evaluate solutions against design criteria
descriptors.description: discuss how existing and student solutions satisfy the design criteria and user stories
descriptors.knowledge: Students can discuss how existing digital systems satisfy identified needs for known users (AC9TDI2P03). They have discussed fit-for-purpose at a general level. They have not yet evaluated solutions explicitly against design criteria and user stories as structured evaluation tools.
elaborations: describing the way familiar digital systems allow the user to perform tasks, for example discussing how a family member could place an order online for something they cannot buy locally

discussing how a digital solution meets the different needs of users, for example how maps help people to locate places in the community or interactive store directories help shoppers to find a particular store in a shopping centre
making judgements on their digital solutions against the design criteria and user stories, for example how high their friends score in the game they created to help them learn what is recyclable
reflecting on how the systems in the school help it run, for example how the librarian keeps track of books borrowed

nodes.label: Describing what a solution does for users
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe what an existing digital solution does and who it helps
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot describe what a solution does for users cannot perform criteria evaluation in N2 — evaluation requires knowing what the solution actually does before checking it against criteria.
criteria: Names at least one task the solution helps users complete
Identifies the user group the solution is designed for

width.minimum: Describe one existing digital solution and explain what task it helps users complete
width.typical: Describe how familiar digital solutions (maps, online orders, interactive directories) allow users to complete specific tasks; identify who benefits and what need each solution addresses
wider: Investigate how a digital solution used in a First Nations community context (e.g. GPS tools for ranger land management) helps specific users — describe what the tool does and who it helps in that context
Describe how library management systems help different users (librarians tracking loans, students finding books) — discuss how the same solution serves different user needs simultaneously

nodes.label: Evaluating against design criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can check a solution against specific design criteria and state whether each criterion is met with a reason
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who evaluate by general impression rather than criterion-by-criterion reasoning cannot engage with N3's user story evaluation — both require the same structured judgement move applied to different frameworks.
criteria: States clearly whether a criterion is met
Gives a reason that references a specific feature of the solution, not just a general impression

width.minimum: Given a solution and one or two criteria, state whether each criterion is met and give one reason
width.typical: Evaluate an existing or student solution against a set of design criteria; for each criterion, state whether it is met and provide a reason; identify criteria the solution meets well and criteria it partially or does not meet
wider: Evaluate a digital solution against criteria that include accessibility or equity considerations — for example, a solution that works well for urban users but fails for users in areas with limited connectivity
Evaluate a student-created game against criteria from both the designer's and a classmate's perspective — discuss how the same solution can be judged differently depending on who is evaluating

modes.reason: Evaluation against criteria requires students to make a criterion-by-criterion judgement move rather than a general impression. Scaffolding the process (identify the criterion → check the solution against it → state whether it is met → give a reason) prevents students from evaluating by opinion alone.

nodes.label: Evaluating against user stories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can check a solution against a user story and discuss how well it meets the user's need and purpose
criteria: References both the user's need and purpose when evaluating
Identifies at least one thing the solution does well and one gap or limitation

width.minimum: Given a solution and one user story, discuss whether the solution meets the user's need and purpose
width.typical: Evaluate existing and student solutions against user stories for different contexts; discuss how well the solution meets both the need and the purpose (the 'so that' part) of the user story; identify gaps between what was designed and what was needed
wider: Evaluate a solution from the perspective of a user story you did not write — for example, evaluate a classmate's game against their user story and discuss whether the solution meets needs you might not have anticipated
Discuss a case where a solution meets the stated need but not the underlying purpose — for example, a tool that works technically but is too complex for the actual user to use

modes.reason: Students commonly evaluate whether the need is met but overlook the 'so that' purpose. Evaluating across different user stories — especially others' user stories — builds the habit of checking both what a solution does and whether it achieves the intended outcome.

This node integrates the design criteria evaluation from node 2 with user story evaluation — applying both simultaneously to assess a solution from multiple lenses. The integration is the learning: criteria and user stories together give a more complete evaluation than either alone.

descriptors.title: Create content with conventions
descriptors.description: use the core features of common digital tools to create, locate and communicate content, following agreed conventions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use basic features of digital tools to create, locate and communicate content (AC9TDI2P04). They have used digital tools for simple content creation. They have not yet worked with agreed conventions, information hierarchies, or search strategies for finding suitable sources.
elaborations: discussing and creating as a class a set of steps they need to follow to safely find information online
using an online search engine to find suitable sources to create and communicate information, following agreed steps, for example creating a presentation on life cycles
grouping, naming and itemising objects using a logical hierarchy, for example creating a section of a virtual library or virtual supermarket using folders and files
using autocomplete features in text authoring tools; for example, using suggestions in a word processor to complete words or sentences, or using predictive text in SMS or messaging apps

nodes.label: Finding information online safely
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow agreed steps to find information online using a search engine
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not internalised safe search steps will bypass them under time pressure in N3 content creation tasks — the habit must be consolidated before it is needed automatically in a production context.
criteria: Follows agreed steps without being prompted
Selects a source that is appropriate for the task

width.minimum: Use a search engine to find information for a purpose following at least two agreed steps (e.g. use safe search, check the source is suitable)
width.typical: Follow a class-agreed set of steps for safe online information search; evaluate whether a source is suitable before using it; create a presentation or document drawing on located information
wider: Investigate how search results differ when using different keywords — discuss how word choice affects what is found and why some searches return unsuitable results
Compare how First Nations Australian community resources are represented in search results — discuss issues of representation and how to locate reliable culturally appropriate sources

modes.reason: Agreed steps for safe online search need to become habitual, not just known. Fluency and consistent application of safe practices — not breadth — is what matters at this node.

nodes.label: Organising content with hierarchies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can group, name and organise files and folders using a logical hierarchy
criteria: Files are placed in folders that match their content category
Folder and file names clearly indicate what is inside

width.minimum: Create at least two folders with appropriate names and place files in the correct folder using a provided logical structure
width.typical: Design and apply a logical folder and file hierarchy for a class project; name folders and files consistently; explain why a given structure makes sense for the type of content
wider: Design a file hierarchy for a virtual library or virtual supermarket with multiple categories and subcategories — explain the organisational logic and how someone unfamiliar with the structure could navigate it
Compare a flat file structure with a hierarchical one for the same set of files — discuss which is easier to navigate and why hierarchy helps with larger collections

modes.reason: Students often create file names and folder structures without reasoning about navigability. The reasoning scaffold — 'what category does this belong to? what would someone search for to find it?' — builds an organisational logic rather than arbitrary grouping.

nodes.label: Using core tool features to create and communicate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use core features of a digital tool (including autocomplete) to create and communicate content following agreed conventions
criteria: Applies at least two agreed conventions in produced content
Content communicates the intended information clearly

width.minimum: Use a digital tool to create content for a purpose, applying at least one agreed convention (e.g. appropriate file name, correct folder, use of autocomplete)
width.typical: Create and communicate content using core tool features across different formats (presentations, documents, messages); apply agreed conventions consistently; use autocomplete features in text authoring tools appropriately
wider: Create content in a tool that is unfamiliar — apply the conventions learned in familiar tools and discuss which transferred and which required adjustment
Create content for a specific audience beyond the classroom (e.g. a presentation for parents or a guide for a younger class) — discuss how conventions change depending on the audience and purpose

modes.reason: Core tool features (file saving, naming conventions, autocomplete, folder use) need to be built across multiple tools and formats before they become transferable. Students who only practise in one tool often cannot apply conventions in a new one — repertoire across formats is the target.

descriptors.title: Share content and collaborate
descriptors.description: use the core features of common digital tools to share content, plan tasks, and collaborate, following agreed behaviours, supported by trusted adults
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use basic features of digital tools to share content and collaborate, demonstrating agreed behaviours guided by trusted adults (AC9TDI2P05). They have shared content in simple, supervised contexts. They have not yet used digital tools to plan tasks collaboratively or manage shared content across a group project.
elaborations: using an agreed folder to make it easy for students to collaborate on shared content in a group project
demonstrating safe sharing of content with a select audience, for example sharing a holiday adventure without revealing exact dates, specific names or other personal information

listening to others when participating in online environments to share content, for example respecting the rights of others by taking turns to suggest and add words or images to a factual slide deck to share with the teacher
interacting cooperatively in a group in an online environment to plan and complete a task, for example writing and responding to others' views on canteen products

using digital tools to plan an event as a class, for example jointly creating a class survey to help plan an end-of-year party, where responses conform to the class's accepted behavioural expectations

nodes.label: Sharing content selectively and safely
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share content with a specific, appropriate audience while keeping personal information appropriately private
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not developed contextual sharing judgement will make inappropriate disclosures in N2 and N3 collaborative tasks — knowing what to share with which audience is prerequisite to participating safely in any collaborative digital activity.
criteria: Shares content only with the agreed audience
Does not include specific personal details (exact dates, specific names, location) in shared content

width.minimum: Share content with an agreed audience (e.g. a class folder, the teacher) without revealing specific personal details
width.typical: Share content in different collaboration contexts (shared folder, class survey, group document); explain which details should be kept private when sharing with different audiences; demonstrate agreed behaviours when sharing
wider: Discuss a scenario where content shared for a legitimate purpose (e.g. sharing a holiday adventure) could inadvertently reveal personal information — identify what should be removed and why
Compare the audience reach of different sharing methods (shared folder vs link vs public post) — discuss which is appropriate for different collaboration contexts

modes.reason: Students often focus on whether they are allowed to share rather than what information sharing reveals. Different sharing contexts (class only, school, public) help students develop a contextual understanding of appropriate sharing rather than a binary 'allowed/not allowed' rule.

nodes.label: Using digital tools to plan tasks collaboratively
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a digital tool to plan and organise a collaborative task with peers
criteria: Makes at least one substantive contribution to the shared planning activity
Follows agreed behaviours when interacting with peers in the digital environment

width.minimum: Contribute to a shared planning document or survey to help organise a group task, following agreed steps
width.typical: Use digital tools to jointly plan an event or task (e.g. a class survey for an end-of-year party, a shared schedule); contribute ideas and respond to others' contributions following agreed behaviours
wider: Plan a multi-step collaborative task using a shared digital tool — assign roles, track progress and update the plan as the task develops; discuss how digital tools make coordination easier for larger groups
Design and administer a class survey using a digital tool — analyse the results collaboratively and use them to make a group decision; discuss how planning tools support group decision-making

modes.reason: Collaborative planning using digital tools is a capability that develops across different tool types and task complexities. Students who only plan using one tool type often cannot transfer the practice. Building repertoire across survey tools, shared documents and scheduling tools strengthens the capability.

nodes.label: Collaborating online with agreed behaviours
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in an online collaboration following agreed behaviours — taking turns, respecting others' contributions, and adding to shared content constructively
criteria: Adds content to a shared digital space following agreed behaviours
Responds to others' contributions in a way that builds on rather than ignores them

width.minimum: Participate in one collaborative online task (e.g. adding to a shared slide deck or document), following at least two agreed behaviours
width.typical: Participate in collaborative online tasks across different formats; listen to and respond to others' contributions; add content that builds on what others have contributed rather than replacing or ignoring it
wider: Collaborate on a task with students from a different class or year level using digital tools — discuss how agreed behaviours need to be explicitly established when collaborating with people you do not know well
Reflect on a collaborative experience and identify one thing that went well and one that could be improved — discuss how agreed behaviours help resolve conflicts in online collaboration

modes.reason: Agreed behaviours in online collaboration need to transfer across tools and audiences. Students who only practise within their own familiar class context may not understand why behaviours need to be re-established with new collaborators or in new tools.

descriptors.title: Memorised passwords
descriptors.description: access their school account using a memorised password and explain why it should be easy to remember, but hard for others to guess
descriptors.knowledge: Students can access their school account using a recorded username and password (AC9TDI2P06). They know that accounts require credentials. They have not yet memorised credentials independently or reasoned about what makes a password strong (easy to remember, hard to guess).
elaborations: recalling their school username and password from memory to login to a school laptop or desktop
explaining how keeping a password secret prevents others from accessing their data, for example how their work is saved in their account and can only be accessed using their secret password
exploring techniques to create an easy to remember and hard to guess password, for example creating a password using 3 unrelated but easy to remember words

nodes.label: Why passwords keep accounts private
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why keeping a password private protects their data
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not connect password secrecy to data protection (treating it as just a rule) cannot reason about what makes a password strong in N2 — the 'hard to guess' criterion only makes sense if students understand what guessing enables.
